previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell activation syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and single-vessel coronary artery disease was admitted for progressive chest pain lasting four days, atypical for ischemia. She denied a mast cell flare but requested her usual IV medications. Evaluation showed no myocardial necrosis on serial troponins, unchanged EKG, and a retrocardiac opacity on chest X-ray likely due to atelectasis. Her cardiac catheterization from an outside hospital revealed a 90% ostial stenosis in a diagonal branch of the LAD and a 70% mid-LAD lesion, but no urgent revascularization was indicated. She was continued on medical therapy for CAD, including aspirin, statin, beta-blocker, and nitrate, with cardiology follow-up planned to discuss CABG. Mast cell regimen was maintained with oral antihistamines and a one-time IV Benadryl. She improved symptomatically and was discharged home with stable vital signs and a plan for outpatient follow-up with cardiology and pulmonology.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ female with substernal chest pain who is two-month out
from a CABG.

STUDY:  PA and lateral chest radiograph.

COMPARISON:  ___ chest radiograph and ___ chest
CTA.

FINDINGS:  The right Port-A-Cath reservoir projects over the right chest and
is currently accessed; the catheter tip ends in the lower SVC.  There has been
interval placement of sternotomy wires, which are intact.  The heart size is
within normal limits and the mediastinal hilar contours do not appear widened.
Calcified AP window node again seen.  The lungs demonstrate left bailar
opacity which is more linear in configuration on the lateral view.  There is
no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  Left costophrenic angle opacity, somewhat linear on the lateral
view, more suggestive of atelectasis or scarring, less likely small focus of
consolidation.  No pleural effusion.
